title: The band playing quietly
summary: The band achieved extremely soft dynamics, with Barker's guitar loudest, and Blumberg calls it the greatest jazz he heard.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: No, but I'll tell you something I wanted to remember about this band, that they achieved this terrific thing of playing so quietly that you could just barely hear the band. The loudest instrument in the band, and this wasn't at first now, but toward the end of the engagement, the loudest instrument in the band was Danny Barker's guitar, an unamplified guitar, and you could hear it ringing through the whole hall.
The whole bunch was playing that song.
And everybody else was playing below the guitar. You'd hear the piano every now and then bang, a couple notes, and the guitar chomping away, but everybody else was playing quieter than that.
How long would they keep that up? How many choruses?
Well, it seemed to me that they did it for half an evening, the last half of an evening.
One number after another, the whole thing.

The whole thing would just be so, they just got it down on a level of such delicate dynamics, and the audience just fit into this, just responded to this so beautifully. Nobody spoke, and everybody was just dancing, just caught up in a kind of hypnotic mood of
the whole thing. Even the last chorus they wouldn't blare out on it.

Oh no, even the last chorus would be real quiet. It would fade away. And you could really hear the dancers' feet shuffling on the floor. Every now and then one of the musicians in the band would swell up, like the bass player would get louder, and then get sink down, or maybe the trombone would swell, and then it would come back. But it had a very strange, dreamy effect. It started to get to the point where you couldn't be sure whether you were actually hearing the clarinet play a phrase, or whether you imagined it. It just went into the realm of magic. And I never heard a band do that. I understand Kid Horry's band did something like that in California.
Yeah, they would do things almost like that. I heard them almost that way. Not much, because I never heard them at their very best, but I heard them pretty good.
I'm telling you, that to me was the greatest jazz I ever heard, because it just was completely effortless, and it just seemed to be, it seemed to transcend the ordinary level of type of music.
What type of pieces were they playing? It wouldn't be Tiger Ragg and that?

No, these were the dance tunes, like Please, or Out of Nowhere, and the things that they did for dancing with that band, the fairly slow things or medium things. Yeah. But even the fast thing, well they did Sister Kate very quietly. I remember Sister Kate. That same style. Yeah, yeah. So relaxed. The band was so, and the thing, I'll never forget it, that several of us were standing near the door at the end of that evening, I guess that was the last evening of the last dance there, and the band, I guess Bunk was playing Goodnight Ladies, or Till We Meet Again, that's the thing, Till We Meet Again. Yeah, here's the thing, sign off. And it was a real quiet thing, and everybody in the place was dancing out of the door, they actually danced on the street, you know, and it was really terrific.
